title: Change risks and the limits of cost controls

opening.headline: Identifies points with increasing risk and cost of change within the scope of each control measure, even when control measures are in place.
body: Even in a team that has quality gates, budget alerts, and bundle deployments, quality and cost issues may suddenly arise simultaneously. This happens because each mechanism is designed to block only within a specific scope.

In this class, we distinguish between blocking and not blocking actions by category, examine the differences between alerts and restrictions, and explore the role of recoverable releases. We analyze a case where a control passed evaluation but incurred significant cost, confirming the design of layered controls.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The scope and limitations can be distinguished by control mechanism.
Can assess the gaps in change risk and cost control

screens.title: Even with control measures in place, there are always points of failure.
screens.lead: Read why risk persists even with a team that has all control measures in place.

visual.alt: This is a diagram showing the defense scopes of various control mechanisms represented by shields of different sizes, with gaps existing between them.

paragraphs: The evaluation gate is in place within the pipeline, budget alerts are configured, and the team has established environment-specific deployments via bundles. Despite having all the necessary controls in place, on some day, the risks and costs of changes suddenly spill out.

The reason is that each mechanism is designed to block only within a specific scope. The evaluation gate reports on the quality of prepared evaluation inputs, the budget alert notifies that a threshold has been exceeded, and bundles deploy the same definition within the defined environment. Activities outside of this scope are not visible to any mechanism.

The problem lies in believing that something is safe simply because we don't know which means block what and which means fail to block. Instead, we must examine how the ranges of different means overlap and diverge.
This course distinguishes between blocking and not blocking based on the method, and addresses a design that stacks alerts, restrictions, and recoverable releases.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The controls for this course include evaluation gates, Databricks budgets, Snowflake resource monitoring and budgeting, and bundle deployments. Each detailed configuration is not covered, with focus instead on scope and limitations.

screens.title: What is it that our control measures cannot block?
screens.lead: Think through each control measure in our team. You don't need to enter an answer; simply selecting a question will reveal the instructor's summary.

items.prompt: Does quality assessment help to keep costs down?
items.answer: It does not prevent this. The evaluation gate blocks promotion based on response quality for evaluation inputs. Even if the response is good, a significant increase in tokens per request can lead to explosive costs, which cannot be filtered solely by quality criteria. Cost metrics must be included as a separate evaluation criterion.

items.prompt: Is the budget alert turning off usage?
items.answer: Alerts alone are not sufficient to stop the system. To terminate usage, a specific action such as Blocking usage or Suspend must be explicitly defined, and such actions only function within their supported scope. Alerts require human response to be effective.

items.prompt: What was the most recent incident involving a control escape?
items.answer: Most are expenditures or changes falling outside the scope of any particular means. For example, AI service costs outside of warehouse monitoring fall into this category. By reviewing what has been overlooked, gaps between means become apparent.

screens.outro: Let's summarize in a table whether things are blocked or not blocked by method.

screens.title: Blocking versus not blocking by control method
screens.lead: While reading the table, distinguish between the scope each method actually covers and the scope it does not cover. Empty spaces indicate areas that need to be filled by other methods.

data.caption: Control mechanism × Blocking × Unable to block
rows: Prevents escalation of changes that do not meet quality standards within the predefined eval case scope.
Cost inflation, inputs outside of evaluation input, quality drift that occurs over time during operation
Tracks monthly spending by account, workspace, and tag scope and notifies via email. Blocks usage when Unity Gateway requests are detected.
Usage scenario where alerts are set only and expenditure does not go through the Unity Gateway

The quality of deployment definition, a deployment that arbitrarily uses an option to bypass approval without rules
data.notes: Looking down the right column of the table reveals the same risks recurring. Cost overruns occur because evaluation gates fail to prevent them, budget alerts fail to stop them, and resource monitors fail to prevent them within AI services. Such risks require mitigation strategies such as incorporating cost metrics into evaluations or imposing overlapping constraints. Bundles include an --auto-approve option that bypasses approval checks; however, using this option without regard for the environment in which it's applied effectively disables safety mechanisms. This illustrates one example of the fact that every solution has a defined scope of support. When reading the table, evaluate based on the scope listed in the right column rather than the name of the mechanism. Even functions with the same name may cover different scopes depending on the platform. Additionally, distinguish between mechanisms that only provide visibility and those that actually enforce restrictions. Usage views only inform you of what has occurred; they do not autonomously halt activity.

screens.outro: Now let's examine how notifications, restrictions, and reversible releases complement each other.

screens.title: Notifications and restrictions, as well as recoverable releases
screens.lead: Toggle between comparing control with notification-centric restrictions and control with overlapping restrictions.

states.label: Alert-centric control
states.body: Alerts are based on human response. If the responsible party is absent or no response mechanism exists, usage continues unimpeded. Lowering thresholds or increasing the number of recipients does not turn alerts into a stopping mechanism. In this state, when a change passes an evaluation gate and increases costs, no one will be aware until the monthly budget threshold is reached, and expenditures continue even after alerts are triggered, as human response is delayed. Visibility exists, but defense relies entirely on human action.

states.label: Control with constraints and recovery
states.body: Limits cause the system to halt in the absence of users. However, since the side effect of limits is service disruption, we must first determine where to apply them. Instead of applying limits across the entire account, narrowing the scope to individual users or workloads allows us to block only a single user's runaway consumption while allowing other services to continue operating. On top of this, we layer in recoverable releases. Bundles reproduce environment-specific deployments via source definitions, validate them beforehand using a validate step, and if issues arise, roll back to the previous stable definition. A pre-approval gate operates before promotion, while monitoring and alerts operate after promotion, filling in each other's gaps. In this structure, one mechanism absorbs risks that another might have missed—this is what "layering" actually means. For example, if a pre-approval step misses a change, real-time alerts catch it; if spending continues beyond the alert, a limit is triggered to halt the service; if issues persist, the entire definition is rolled back via rollback. The effectiveness and side effects of limits depend on where they are applied. Applying limits across the entire account definitively halts spending but stops all services at once. User-level limits only prevent a single user's runaway consumption, while workload-level limits halt only the affected workloads. Snowflake's user-level query quotas apply limits separately per user without aggregation, so when a total budget is required, budgets are applied together. The delay before limits are enforced must also be considered in the design. To account for overspending during this delay, the limit threshold should be set below the user's quota. Guidance messages to be displayed to users when limits are triggered, as well as the responsible personnel who can lift those limits, must also be pre-defined.

screens.outro: Let's apply layered design to real-world scenarios.

screens.title: Case where cost surged despite passing the evaluation gate
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a case where a passed prompt significantly increases costs, step by step. Please click the following arrow to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The new prompt has passed the evaluation gate's criteria and has been promoted. All quality metrics were normal, and the pipeline operated as expected. However, a few days later, the billing usage had increased several times over its usual level.

steps.title: Cause: The request token has increased.
steps.body: The new prompt has been changed to include longer context, significantly increasing the number of tokens used per request. Response quality might have improved instead. It was a change that maintained acceptable quality but increased costs.

steps.title: Why couldn't the gate be blocked?
steps.body: The evaluation gate determines promotion based on quality criteria. Since cost was not included in the evaluation items, it represented a change that needed to be approved from the gate's perspective. The gate did not fail; rather, the cost dimension was outside the scope.

steps.title: Why couldn't the budget be contained?
steps.body: The budget had alerts set only. The alerts triggered only after the threshold was exceeded, and by the time the alerts sounded, significant expenditures had already accumulated. Since there was no limit, calls continued after the alert was triggered. If there was a delay in applying the limit, additional expenditures would have occurred during that delay period.

steps.title: Response and recurrence prevention
steps.body: First, deploy the previous stable definition again using a recoverable release. Then, incorporate cost metrics such as tokens requested in evaluation criteria to make gates aware of cost, and combine user- and workload-level limits to prevent surges even when no human is present. Additionally, a review feature is added to compare costs per request before and after the change point using the usage view. The key takeaway from this incident is not that we should not trust gates, but rather that gates only view one axis.

steps.title: Check: Has the same issue occurred again?
steps.body: To verify whether recurrence prevention has been completed, check three criteria: whether cost metrics are included in the evaluation items, whether limits are applied on a per-user or per-workload basis, and whether a rollback procedure has been actually reviewed at least once. The last criterion is included because if a rollback is only planned and has never been executed, it may not function during an emergency.

screens.outro: Finally, let's sketch a map to identify vulnerabilities within our organization.

screens.title: How to Find Our Vulnerabilities: Step-by-Step Control Guide
screens.lead: When a number marker is selected, descriptions for each area on the control map are displayed. Empty spaces indicate gaps.

visual.alt: In the case of change, there are risks of modification and cost; for heat, there is a control framework established at pre-, real-time, and post-incident stages.

markers.label: Pre-processing stage
markers.title: Tasks handled in the pre-phase
markers.body: The evaluation gate and validate are responsible. The evaluation gate prevents promotion of changes that do not meet quality criteria, and bundle validate confirms beforehand whether the configuration is deployable. However, the pre-phase has the limitation that it only verifies within the scope of prepared inputs and defined boundaries.

markers.label: Real-time stage
markers.title: What is handled by the real-time stage
markers.body: Alerts, limits, and monitoring are responsible. They detect or halt operations when thresholds are exceeded during runtime. Quality alerts are triggered by the continuous evaluation results of online monitors, and cost-related limits include block usage, warehouse shutdowns, and user-specific quotas. Remember that there may be delays between limit application and actual enforcement.

markers.label: Post-stages
markers.title: What is handled in the post-stage
markers.body: Manages usage views aggregation and rollbacks. Breaks down usage data by date, product, team, and workload to identify root causes, and redeployes the previous baseline definition to revert changes. The post-stage serves as the final safety net to mitigate already-occurred incidents.

markers.label: Empty cell
markers.title: An empty space is a vulnerability.
markers.body: For example, if the pre-change cost risk cell is empty, it means there is no means to assess cost impacts before making changes. The cell can be filled with cost indicators such as tokens requested in the evaluation item. If the cell is empty, supplement the scope of the means to address it; however, if a means exists but falls outside the scope, then the expenditure or change will not be protected.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: We summarize the design of stacking controls layer by layer. As you read, sketch out the roadmap for our organization.

paragraphs: Control is layered. Evaluation gates focus only on pre-quality checks, budgeting is alert-driven, and resource monitoring covers only the warehouse scope—thus, no single mechanism can fully mitigate overall risk.
Alerts notify and limits stop. Limits introduce the side effect of service disruption, so they are scoped by user or workload.
The recoverable release is the last safety net. It must be able to redeploy a previous stable definition so that issues overlooked during pre-evaluation and real-time constraints can be mitigated.
When identifying gaps, create a roadmap outlining change risks and cost risks across pre-change, real-time, and post-change stages, and fill in the empty cells.

Going back to the introduction case, what was needed was not a single, more stringent measure, but rather multiple overlapping measures that complement each other. Once a map is drawn out, it becomes clear when introducing a new control measure where exactly a cell should be filled. The map should be updated once every quarter to ensure that newly incurred expenses or changed categories are not missed. Empty cells should not be hidden; instead, they should be shared so the team can collectively view them.

callout.label: inspection questions
callout.text: What is an expenditure or change that falls outside the scope of any of the control measures we use?

checks.q: Pair control measures with the things they fail to prevent.
right: Expenditure not passing through Unity Gateway
checks.explain: Each mechanism covers only a specific range. Features outside this range are not visible, so mechanisms must be paired by type of expenditure or change.
checks.intro: Pair controls with what they do not prevent. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, the boundaries outside each method's scope have been distinguished.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch. Please verify the reference axes of each method: quality, warehouse, gateway.

checks.q: What is needed to halt expenditure spikes even if the responsible person is absent?
options: Alert email with lower threshold value
Increasing the number of alert recipients
Limited operation where the system stops without human intervention
checks.explain: Alerts are based on human response, while constraints halt the system. However, constraints may have side effects leading to service disruption, and these are scoped by user or workload.

wrong.0: Notifications are ineffective if no one sees them.
wrong.1: The receiver may increase, but the alert is not a device that stops.
wrong.3: Post-incident aggregation is used for root cause analysis and does not stop in real time.

checks.intro: Select the condition under which expenditure surge stops even if no supervisor is assigned. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. It should not require any human intervention to pause when absent.
checks.incorrectFeedback: All of these methods require human intervention to be effective. Recall the difference between alerts and restrictions.

checks.q: The new prompt has passed the evaluation gate and been promoted, but the requested tokens have increased, leading to a sharp rise in costs. What is an appropriate response?
options: Remove the evaluation gate and keep only the budget notification.
Include cost metrics in the evaluation criteria and overlay user-specific and workload-specific limits.
Making quality evaluation criteria more stringent also increases costs.
Wait until the budget alert sounds
checks.explain: The evaluation gate did not prevent cost increase because it was focused on quality. Cost indicators were added, overlapping constraints were introduced, and in case of issues, rollback to previous definitions is applied.

wrong.0: The gate's role in preventing premature quality is still necessary.
wrong.2: Quality is a separate axis from cost.
wrong.3: Alerts are triggered only after a threshold is exceeded, and if no limit is set, expenditure continues indefinitely.

checks.intro: Choose your response when costs surge after approval. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Filling in the missing axis and overlapping constraints is the response.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This choice either fails to fill the missing axis or leads to continuous expenditure. First, consider what the gate is observing.

glossary.def: One control mechanism refers to the area actually blocked or alerted.
Notifications inform people, while limits cause the system to halt requests or resources.
Only the quality of the evaluation input range is verified; cost increases and operational drift must be monitored separately.
This is a release designed to allow rolling back to the previous stable definition.

misconceptions.myth: If there is an evaluation gate, costs are also controlled.
misconceptions.fact: The quality gate reviews quality criteria. Since it does not assess costs, cost metrics must be incorporated into the evaluation or separate controls must be established.

misconceptions.myth: Once the budget is set, overspending is impossible.
misconceptions.fact: Alerts alone will not suffice. Blocking only operates when limited actions are specified within the supported scope.

misconceptions.myth: The more methods you have, the fewer vulnerabilities there are.
misconceptions.fact: If the ranges do not overlap, empty spaces remain. This is not a numerical issue but a range issue.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Control is stacked layer by layer.
The evaluation gate covers only pre-quality checks, budgeting is alert-centric, and monitoring covers only the warehouse scope.
Notifications inform and limits stop, with recoverable releases as the final safety net.
Place changes and cost risks on a phased roadmap and fill in the blanks.

Going back to the introduction case, what was needed was not a single, more stringent measure, but rather multiple layers that complement each other. Once a map is drawn, it becomes clear when introducing a new control measure, exactly which cell to fill.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Among the control measures we use, is there any expenditure or change that falls outside the scope of any particular measure?
